ORLANDO, Florida — For 18 months, United Parcel Service management has talked about shedding unprofitable e-commerce volume to concentrate on more complex, premium services in sectors like B2B distribution, healthcare, automotive and small enterprises. Many hear that to mean UPS intends to walk away from B2C final-mile delivery space, now crowded with lower-cost competitors, especially after phasing out 50% of its business with Amazon .
Meanwhile, the shipping giant recently issued a news release in which it described a new global operating model centered on providing integrated logistics services as the company continues its “evolution” from a small package carrier.
Analysts question whether UPS ( NYSE: UPS ) can successfully morph into an integrated logistics provider if it shrinks parcel volume. And industry consultant Satish Jindel suspects there are other motives behind the messaging, arguing the company has no intention of exiting any part of the parcel business.
“I think it’s a very difficult needle to thread. They’re a parcel carrier. Plain and simple,” Richard Metzler, an industry veteran who has held high-level executive positions at companies like DHL Express, Greatwide Logistics, XPO and uShip, said in a phone interview. “Is Supply Chain Services a serious logistics business? For sure. But in my opinion, it will be tough to backfill what they exit in parcel with just logistics, small-and-medium businesses, heavyweight and healthcare.”
And since Amazon is rapidly moving to serve those market segments with its third-party freight, distribution, fulfillment and parcel shipping service, under the Amazon Supply Chain Services banner, profit margins won’t be safe in logistics either, he added
In early August, Jindel warned negotiations on the next contract for more than 300,000 van and truck drivers and package handlers will turn into a tectonic clash that reshapes the parcel shipping sector , with either UPS becoming the top dog or getting overlapped by rival couriers, depending on how the talks play out.
UPS’s labor costs are so out of whack with the rest of the industry because of the lucrative 2023 contract the Teamsters secured that UPS is becoming unaffordable for retail shippers, according to many industry watchers.
Jindel is now going further, predicting that UPS will welcome a strike by the Teamsters union and its combative boss Sean O’Brien, who is already drawing red lines that could easily trigger a work stoppage in 2028, so it can reset its cost structure.
The emphasis on revenue quality over sheer parcel volume is actually a smokescreen to keep parcel delivery competitors, like FedEx and Amazon, off guard so they don’t prepare for a driver exodus when Teamsters workers go on strike, enabling UPS to hire drivers from competitors and reset its cost structure. That would allow UPS to again dominate the parcel market like it did in the 1990s, he opined in an interview.
Although UPS downsized its domestic parcel network — eliminating 150 sort centers, 30,000 positions and 50 million labor hours — to align with lower volumes from shedding Amazon business, it wouldn’t be investing more than $8 billion over four years to automate facilities, if it planned to stop delivering from fulfillment centers to consumers’ doorsteps, Jindel explained.
UPS is trying to make people believe they are pulling out of short-haul parcel delivery. “They are not. This is a Trojan horse to misguide competitors and the Teamsters,” the founder and president of ShipMatrix told FreightWaves.
ShipMatrix supports hundreds of shippers with parcel visibility, analytics, invoice processing, auditing and carrier selection. Jindel has a strong track record of predicting industry events or making recommendations that eventually are adopted, including the spinoff of FedEd Freight and retailers’ overreaction to consumer interest in free, superfast delivery.
In the Aug. 31 news release downplaying the parcel operations, UPS also named Matt Guffey as chief U.S. domestic officer, with responsibility over all parcel and delivery business units: small package, non-union subsidiaries Roadie and Happy Returns, The UPS Stores and Mail Innovations (the company’s consolidation program with the U.S. Postal Service for lightweight parcels).
UPS purchased Roadie in 2021 for $548 million. The carrier handles same-day, urgent shipments that don’t go through the parent company’s parcel sortation network. Instead, the crowdsourced delivery platform instead picks up orders from brand-name stores and delivers them to homes and businesses, with independent drivers providing their own vehicles.
Jindel said the reorganization under Guffey suggests that UPS intends all five units will eventually utilize non-union workers because, for the first time, management has brought all the parcel services under one executive. It will allow use of a fully integrated parcel network to meet customers’ needs at the lowest cost by placing the right parcel in the right network.
The reorganization aligns with a scenario he floated last November , in which UPS proposes that Roadie carry out all B2C deliveries from UPS Stores, while Teamster drivers handle shuttle runs between package hubs and the UPS retail outlet — a nonstarter for the Teamsters that would likely tee up a strike. UPS will be able to manage a strike without huge damage if Roadie has plenty of freelance workers signed up on its app in advance to deliver packages and management bringing packages to the UPS Stores.
UPS officials privately caution not to read too much into the Aug. 31 statement: Small package is not going away. Core competency is now directed at transportation moves that require multiple services, but also feed into the small package network, where the driver still needs to deliver the product to a home or business, and customers view UPS as a partner in the end-to-end logistics process.
“Our number one priority is to move the right packages and the right mix of volume through our network. The market has changed and we’re adapting to it,” CEO Carol Tomé said in the company’s second quarter earnings briefing.
“We’re overturning the old industry assumption that scale alone drives profitability. Instead, we’re focused on premium segments. … Our strategy is working. We’re seeing favorable mix improvements with small-and-medium business and B2B volume representing a larger share of total U.S. volume and … meaningful revenue per piece growth. … We’re winning through innovative and differentiated capabilities,” she said.
Being selective about which shipments to accept means lower revenue, but UPS — and FedEx, for that matter — is partly making up for that money by frequently introducing a broad range of surcharges throughout the contract year, a relatively new tactic for increasing revenue-per-package.
Mixed opinions on strike chances
The fact that Teamsters chief Sean O’Brien has used inflammatory language to disparage UPS and insist it accept more union demands in the next contract, while suggesting a labor stoppage is almost inevitable, is striking two years before the current labor contract expires.
Not everyone is convinced as Jindel that a strike will occur, while seeming to acknowledge it will be a close call. Their comments reflect a broader nervousness across the carrier and shipping community that a UPS shutdown is possible.
James Cochrane, chief executive officer of the Package Shippers Association, said UPS has to do something to rebalance its costs with the market.
“The last [contract] didn’t end well for them. Their cost to serve went very high. The people that deliver are hardworking individuals, but there’s such a difference between people that are delivering packages making $50,000 a year and those making $150,000. I don’t know how sustainable that is,” he said during a keynote address at Parcel Forum 26 here last month.
The Teamsters strike of UPS in 1997 was damaging to the company because it took time to regain business from FedEx, he recalled.
“I don’t think there’ll be a strike, but I don’t envy UPS having to negotiate that one because very rarely do things [contract terms] move backwards. They’re at a high number now, and so I worry about their long-term longevity with that kind of cost. I would love to see them maybe get a distributed environment where some of the new employees have a lower base for a period of time,” Cochrane said.
Teamsters drivers cost about $65 per hour — total compensation when all healthcare and other benefits are included with the $49 hourly rate for senior drivers — compared to FedEx drivers who earn about $35 to $39 per hour on average for total compensation.
Regional carriers that heavily rely on contract fleets or gig workers spend about $15 per hour, or less, on last-mile delivery drivers, experts say.
“The real battleground in 2028 might be a show down over Roadie. UPS spent $548 million to buy Roadie and the time may be approaching to pull it off the shelf. Decoupling middle-mile Teamster haulage from gig-based final-mile delivery isn’t just an option for UPS — it is probably the only mathematical reality that allows them to remain competitive,” wrote Metzler in the comment section of a FreightWaves article about UPS.
Vincent D’Amato, chief sales officer at startup carrier Gofo, said his attitude toward a potential strike is colored by previous cries of wolf that never materialized when UPS contracts came up for renewal.
“I’m not saying there’s zero chance. I”m saying I don’t really buy into the hype because I spent 17 years at FedEx and every cycle it would come up and we’d be told to go out to the customer base and tell them they need to lock in volume now because if it gets closer we’re not going to take volume. And it never really happened,” he said on the sidelines of the conference. “I just feel as though there’s always talk about the strike. I just don’t think it’s a significant likelihood that it would happen, enough where it would create a panic in the market.”
If UPS workers did walk off the job it would severely hurt businesses and create shipping delays, he added.
“It would be catastrophic for the parcel market. Most of these alternative providers can’t handle that volume. They would be inundated. FedEx would be very disciplined about what they would and wouldn’t take at what price,” said D’Amato. “Maybe Amazon or the USPS could absorb some of it.”
Can UPS ignore last-mile delivery?
Despite UPS’s public position about being very intentional in only accepting high- margin , multi-zone, specialized shipments that fit their profile, analysts say the company can’t afford to abandon a key segment of the market when its goal is to provide integrated logistics solutions.
Integrated logistics, by definition, means having one’s own assets and network, said Jindel.
“It can’t be either, or, especially because consumers and businesses require both” B2C and B2B shipping capabilities that, for example, can get pharmaceuticals to someone’s house or to a hospital, said Joanne Strong, senior manager and warehouse management system practice lead at Deloitte, during a panel discussion. “The market is very dynamic and there are all these operating models going after the same customer based on what that means for them at that moment.”
Over-the-road trailers are parked at a UPS sort center in Portland, Oregon on June 15, 2026. (Photo: Eric Kulisch/FreightWaves)
Metzler agreed that cherry picking a big piece of the market won’t work because shippers won’t give all of the quality packages to one carrier.
“Carriers are going to go after where the biggest margins are. But you have to be able to offer those [last-mile] services to really make it work. They have got to build their physical networks with freight. They need volume to make those operationally successful,” Chris Kina, senior director analyst for logistics, customer fulfillment and network design at Gartner, said at the event. New technology, added, is going to enable more carriers to expand their service offerings.
Focusing on premium market segments is risky when the line between commerce and package delivery is disappearing, as platforms like DoorDash and Uber expand from restaurant and grocery delivery to deliver orders from big and small stores, including brands like Costco and Ace Hardware, while retailers like Walmart deliver more packages on their own, said Nate Skiver, the founder of LPF Spend Management, on LinkedIn.
The amount of available package volume for pure-play couriers will shrink, as a result. “Which begs the question: Is there enough ‘premium’ volume for both UPS and FedEx?” he said.
D’Amato said that UPS would have to significantly scale down its network if it were going to push out B2C delivery.
“ They may have painted themselves into a corner with the last Teamsters contract. Plus, Sean O’Brien has made it abundantly clear the next contract will be no fun and will close the gaps on Roadie, UPS Stores and Supply Chain Services” Metzler said. “With the fixed cost of the UPS network, it is hard to see how they can get to the Promised Land with lower package density on any given route.”
Not too early for contingency planning
Some businesses are beginning to realize the need for contingency plans as awareness increases about the strong potential of a strike at UPS, and the chain reaction it could set off across the parcel industry, parcel shipping consultants say.
Jindel said customers are asking about how to prepare for any potential labor disruption, including how to incorporate alternative carriers in their automated manifesting and label-generation systems, after reading his Aug. 11 commentary warning about the UPS-Teamsters negotiating cliff.
Analysts say the proliferation of surcharges for peak season, fuel, large packages, non-urban delivery areas and other conditions has irritated shippers, making them more open to using alternative carriers.
“Carrier diversification is already a focus for many shippers because of rising costs and service concerns, and the potential for another UPS strike adds to that conversation,” Robyn Meyer, senior vice president, parcel strategy and solutions at Transportation Insight, told FreightWaves.
“It’s not a major concern just yet. I think the biggest lesson from 2023 is that shippers can’t wait until the last minute. Alternative carriers have limited capacity, and building those relationships takes time,” she said.
Shippers should be engaging with other carriers so that their warehouse management and transportation management systems are integrated and ready to exchange information if that becomes necessary, the ShipMatrix chief recommended. Carriers will be overwhelmed onboarding new accounts if shippers wait until 2028.
“Your packages will be piling up. You won’t be able to ship,” Jindel said.
Parcel shippers also have to worry about the financial impact of shifting volume away from UPS and potentially affecting existing contract incentives.
“I expect we’ll see more conversations around this throughout 2027, especially among larger shippers with significant UPS volume,” said Meyer.
Some shippers, in an effort to maintain flexibility to divert packages if a labor disruption occurs, are asking UPS to include clauses in contract renewals that waive volume requirements for discounted rates, Jindel said.

Plymouth Superbird Crashed Its Nose at Car Meet, Insurance Paid $30K, the Car Sold for $170K
105 photos
Photo: Facebook/John Gardoski
Usually, sellers who have something valuable will price their possessions around 10% to 25% above their real target. Well, it doesn't go like that when Plymouth Superbirds are on the table. The owner of 22 years of this 1970 U-code 'Bird asked $225 this past summer. He just let it go for (a lot) less. The classic car market is unpredictable, and this pristine aerodynamic warrior serves as evidence.
This exact automobile is known among classic vehicle enthusiasts as the “Car Village Superbird .” It was acquired by a previous owner in 1980 from a dealership called Car Village located in Lebanon, Pennsylvania. That person traded in a Dodge truck to get it and subsequently kept the prized machine stored safely inside a detached two-car garage in Maryland from 1981 all the way until 2004.
In April 2004, the seller purchased the vehicle and meticulously maintained it over a remarkable 22-year period. As a result, this 1970 Plymouth Superbird had only two caretakers over the last 46 years, making its history highly transparent. The odometer shows just 45,000 original miles, while the car itself retains its matching numbers 440 cubic-inch V8 engine and a clean Delaware title.
This particular unit boasts the 440 Super Commando engine with a single 4-barrel carburetor, a configuration that found its way into 1,084 vehicles. When it comes to transmission choices, Plymouth matched 618 of those standard 440 V8 models with the 3-speed Torqueflite automatic gearbox, just like the column-shifted automatic seen here. Furthermore, documentation indicates this is the 993rd Superbird built out of the limited production run.
Photo: Hagerty Marketplace Visually, the car presents beautifully in its original factory Vitamin C paint. Records indicate that a reported 278 Superbirds were ordered in this striking, high-impact color. In 2005, the owner treated the solid, rust-free body to a high-quality repaint, fitted new decals, installed fresh door handles, and mounted a new rear bumper. The original factory vinyl top impressively remains right in its place.
Unfortunately, the original aerodynamic nosecone suffered damage at a car show some years ago. Hagerty Insurance paid out over $30,000 to fix the front end. The owner acquired a rare new old stock replacement nose from Superbird expert Doug Schellinger, and Mike Mancini from American Muscle Car Restorations installed and painted it. The only other metalwork involved fixing a bent lower passenger quarter panel.
Inside the cabin, this vehicle features an incredibly rare, untouched white vinyl bench seat interior. The seller notes that even the carpet is original to the car, and they simply could not find another Superbird with this specific white bench configuration. In 2005, a brand-new headliner and rear package tray were added, while the dashboard displays only one minor 3-inch hairline crack from a previous painting incident.
Photo: Hagerty Marketplace There is also some loose stitching on the passenger seat, which the owner cleverly covers with the original seatbelts during shows to preserve the factory material. Other interior imperfections include dash lights that recently quit working and a disconnected aftermarket Sun tachometer. The windshield washer bottle is also disconnected, and the original trunk jacks are missing, but the meep-meep horn and pop-up headlights work flawlessly every time.
Mechanically, the owner wanted a dependable cruiser and heavily invested in proper maintenance. In 2005, they replaced the fuel tank, fuel lines, brakes, calipers, hoses, master cylinder, radiator, water pump, thermostat, belts, and the alternator. They also swapped the transmission fluid , installed a new transmission pan, and fitted a new exhaust system with factory-style tips, making sure to save most of the original replaced components.
This classic ride sits on 14-inch Rallye wheels wrapped in Goodyear Polyglas raised letter tires from Coker Tire, which only have about 5,000 miles on them. To improve reliability, the seller installed an Edelbrock carburetor and upgraded the ignition system to an MSD electronic unit.
Photo: Hagerty Marketplace Both the original carburetor and distributor (together with a lot of other miscellaneous original parts) were set aside in boxes. the next owner has everything needed for an accurate factory restoration, should he wish to make it so.
It’s not too often that we come across a Superbird owner that actually likes to drive his car AND actually drives it. Understandable, since these cars weren’t exactly what we’d call abundant. For the 1970 model year, Plymouth produced a minimum of 1,920 Superbird units. Then they halted the program. Forever. The exact production volume is debated (and datable), mainly due to sloppy records that don’t clarify the misunderstandings.
The cars were built to satisfy NASCAR homologation rules and win back legendary driver Richard Petty, who had jumped ship to Ford for the 1969 season, after ChryCo refused to make him a Plymouth similar to the 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona. The standard motor in the Superbird was the U-code 440-4 Super Commando. The top tier 426 Hemi engine accounted for just 135 units, while the 440 Six-Barrel version was installed in 716 examples.
Photo: Hagerty Marketplace When discussing classic muscle car values, Plymouth Superbirds command respect. The current auction record for a 1970 Plymouth Superbird belongs to a rare 426 Hemi model that sold for an astounding 1,650,000 USD at a 2022 Las Vegas auction. While the 440 automatic examples do not reach those 7-figure heights, the market benchmark and median sale value for a 440-powered 1970 Superbird currently hovers around 222,000 USD in 2026.
Considering those market values, the initial $225,000 asking price made logical sense for such a beautifully documented, numbers-matching survivor. The car comes with two original broadcast sheets, the original fender tag, and a matching chassis number stamped directly on the radiator support. Despite its compelling history, absolute rarity, and an exceptional maintenance record, the final auction transaction brought an unexpected twist, concluding at a surprising figure.
Ultimately, the buyer secured an incredible deal on this legendary winged warrior. The final sale price landed at exactly 170,000 USD, though the buyer ultimately paid 181,900 USD after factoring in the required auction fees (Hagerty charger 7%). Selling for 55,000 USD under the original asking price perfectly reflects the unpredictable nature of the current collector car market. Regardless, this Vitamin C Superbird remains a magnificent piece of American automotive history.

Just when I thought I was out, they pull me back in. Remember that Red Mist Metallic ZR1X from yesterday that sold for “just” $315,000? I was quite excited about it, seeing how it was the cheapest used ZR1X ever to hit the auction block. Well, rest assured ZR1X flippers, you can still make a “killing” by unloading your flagship Vette on the used market.
Case in point, this 2027 ZR1X Convertible, which by the way is brand spanking new with just 19 miles on the clock (delivery miles). It sold for $390,000, plus a buyer’s fee, courtesy of a dealer out of Palmdale, California.
The best part is that because the car was never previously sold to a private party, that means that the warranty is intact, so the new owner can sleep well knowing that they’re covered in case something goes wrong – there have been a few reliability issues reported with the ZR1X.
As far as I’m concerned, when you add up the warranty, the spec, the delivery mileage, and everything else you can think of, that’s how you justify spending nearly $400,000 on a Corvette in 2026. Would I have done it if it was my own money? Almost certainly not. Not even if I could easily afford it.
It’s not a financial issue, but more of a moral issue for me. Look at it this way, I can easily afford a flagship phone, but if that flagship phone isn’t considerably better than the next model in line, there’s no way I’d pay nearly twice as much just to get the latest and greatest, not unless the price is somehow justified.
As things stand right now, there’s too much of a price gap on the used market between the ZR1X and the “regular” ZR1, and not enough of a performance gap. It’s as simple as that.
Back to this car, aside from its Black exterior, it also comes with several carbon fiber accents courtesy of the Carbon Fiber Aero Package, plus you’ve got the power-retractable carbon fiber hardtop, LED headlights, front and rear cameras, side air intakes, black exhaust tips, and the optional 20” and 21” carbon fiber wheels rocking Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2R rubber and carbon-ceramic brakes. The combined output is 1,250 horsepower and 973 lb-ft (1,320 Nm) of torque, with everything getting sent to all four wheels via an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic gearbox and an electric AWD system.

The Atlas Mobile Home Slides the Bed Outside for the Ultimate Stargazing Experience
11 photos
Photo: Zook Cabins
Tiny houses, whether standard towable ones or park models, are not to everyone's taste, and that's ok. We're all different and consequently want different things from life, but we can all agree that most tinies employ highly imaginative gimmicks to make up for their compact footprints.
From oversize glazing to entire walls of glass, modular furniture, unexpected layouts, and a surprising amount of everyday functionality, tiny houses use the full range of tricks up a designer's sleeve to create space where none is to be had – or, at best, to create the impression of a bigger volume than there is.
By this measure, The Atlas will seem even more impressive as the first park tiny to feature a mobile bedroom. Instead of using gimmicks to add more space inside or to make the existing footprint feel larger, The Atlas boldly erases the boundary between indoors and outdoors and takes the former out into the latter.
The Atlas is the newest creation from Pennsylvania-based builder Zook Cabins , a specialist in park tinies and ADUs (additional dwelling units). It is also a park tiny, which means that, while it can move, it's supposed to do so only rarely, if ever.
Photo: Zook Cabins Because of its defining feature – Zook Cabins also calls it The Stargazer tiny house – this model sacrifices some home comforts, so it's best suited as a guest house or rental property. In either case, it should be parked on private property and left there.
The Atlas is built on a custom steel chassis with a triple axle and measures 22 feet (6.7 meters) in length and 12 feet (3.6 meters) in width. That said, for it to have that defining feature of the stargazing bed, it must be accompanied by a 10-foot (3-meter) detachable deck, so total length will be at 32 feet (9.7 meters).
Inside, you get 233 square feet (21.6 square meters) of living space divided into two separate rooms: the open-plan bedroom and kitchenette, and the bathroom, which runs the full width of the home and can be accurately described as "spa-like." All of this is highly irregular for a park tiny but, remember, this is no regular park tiny.
Photo: Zook Cabins The main entrance is on the side of the home. At the rear, Zook Cabins installs a glass garage door with manual operation, but you can have it motorized on request. Once you open up this door, you can roll the bed manually on the provided runners, until it's out on the Lunawood premium deck.
The home features a bit of an overhang at the back, but it doesn't provide shelter for the bed. Neither is there a flyscreen included at the back, so, with the gazing at the stars, you will also be braving the elements and whatever critters will want to get inside the home .
Even with the bed in its original position, you still have some moving room inside. Features include a closet space with open shelving and a hanging rod, as well as a 9,000-BTU LG mini-split for heat and AC, and a small kitchenette on the other side. A flip-down metal table is built into the back of the headrest, so you have a dining table or desk space when the bed is out.
Photo: Zook Cabins This comes equipped with a granite sink, a laminate counter, a 4.4 cu-ft fridge underneath, and a bank of drawers and open shelves for storage. It's enough to brew a pot of coffee or tea and maybe to fix something up for a quick breakfast, but it's not the type of galley where you will want to – or could – spend too much time in.
You might in the bathroom, though. Running the full width of the home , it's equipped with a nice walk-in shower with glass doors and tiled walls, a small sink on a vanity with integrated storage, an Envi electric wall heater, and what looks like a regular plumbed toilet.
The manufacturer doesn't offer specifics here because they're not needed: since it's a park model, this home is meant to be hooked up to the grid and utilities.
Photo: Zook Cabins The Atlas comes with Lunawood siding on the exterior and metal roofing, birch plywood interiors with premium vinyl flooring, dimmable LED lights throughout, and a style that's deliberately minimalist and natural. The only contrast comes from the black windows and doors, which, again, is deliberate.
Zook Cabins notes that the home is insulated and is comfortable for year-round use, but take that to mean "except the rolling bed option" because no one would want to open that garage door in the dead of winter. The idea is that you can get some usage out of it even in colder temperatures, even if you won't be using its most striking feature.
Photo: Zook Cabins The Atlas made its debut earlier this month (October) at a local trade event. There is no price tag or starting MSRP attached to it right now, but that's only because Zook Cabins offers customization options and, as such, personalized quotes.

By Alex Lennane
14 October 2026
AI infrastructure shippers, still seeking peak-season capacity, could push air freight rates sharply higher, as demand for servers, chips, and data centre equipment adds pressure to an already firm market.
According to TAC Index, sources have reported that ecommerce customers and other major shippers with product launches had secured peak-capacity, while some AI hyperscalers had yet to book their space.
The warning comes despite a Golden Week dip in TAC’s global Baltic Air Freight Index, which fell 2.1% in the seven days to 12 October, leaving it 24.3% above a year earlier. China’s holiday ended on 7 October.
While overall rates from China to Europe and the US softened over the week, nearly all TAC’s spot rates out of Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Korea rose, with increases particularly evident in recent days.
New analysis of US imports underlines the scale of technology-related demand. Supply chain professor Jason Miller’s seasonal adjustment of Census Bureau trade data showed August air freight imports by weight reaching another record, up 20% year on year, and 42% above the 2023 average.
Computer parts, including GPUs, contributed an additional 12,932 tonnes, compared with August last year, while prepared unrecorded media, including memory, added 11,111 tonnes. Electrical power equipment and insulated wire and cables were also among the leading contributors.
Mr Miller said these categories pointed to the “disproportionate role” of investment in the physical infrastructure supporting AI computing in generating freight demand.
His findings concern US air imports, but forwarder Forto also identified a broad shift towards technology in its third-quarter market analysis.
Semiconductors, AI hardware, servers, and data centre infrastructure were the principal growth drivers, it said, while ecommerce had declined in relative importance.
And the changing demand picture is also influencing how forwarders secure capacity.
Speaking at an industry event in Liège last month, DSV’s global head of airfreight, Stefan Krikken, said forwarders needed to balance firm capacity commitments with more flexible airline bookings and their own flying programmes, taking account of hyperscaler demand and constraints at cargo gateways.
Hyperscaler demand was among the factors shaping those decisions, alongside the ability of gateways to accommodate the cargo.
Morrison Express has also identified growing hyperscaler production in South-east Asia, and exceptionally high Taiwanese volumes as factors prompting a reassessment of its gateways.
However, stronger demand and higher rates may offer carriers less financial relief than the headline figures suggest.
TAC reported that jet fuel prices rose a further 3.1% in the week to 9 October, citing IATA’s Jet Fuel Price Monitor, taking the year-on-year increase to 111.2%. And i n his latest JTD Advisory briefing, founder David Kerr warned that fuel costs were rising faster than freight rates, putting pressure on operating margins.
He expects fuel surcharge resets in the second half of October, and identified four-engine freighters as the aircraft most likely to face pressure to reprice, or be parked.
Published surcharges already illustrate the pressure on shipping costs. Cathay Cargo’s Hong Kong-origin long-haul fuel surcharge rose almost 26%, from HK$11.20 to HK$14.10 (US$1.42-$1.79) per kg, for the first half of October. DHL Air UK’s equivalent charge increased 4.1% week on week, to HK$12.80 per kg for 12–18 October, although it remained below its late-September level.
Japan Airlines will raise its fuel surcharge on domestic exports bound for the Americas and Europe from ¥185 ($1.16) to ¥192 per kg on 16 October, an increase of 3.8%. Its medium-haul and short-haul Asian surcharges will rise by around 4%.
The impact on individual operators will depend on their fuel exposure and ability to recover costs, but the combination adds another pricing risk for shippers seeking remaining peak-season space.
For those AI customers still to secure capacity, the question is how much room remains, and what it will cost.

Sharp increases in rates and extra fees have continued into the fourth quarter, putting 2026 on track to be the most expensive year on record for parcel shipping as carriers strive to maximize revenue, according to the latest market snapshot from investment bank TD Cowen and AFS Logistics.
Analysts say the onslaught of surcharges is spurring businesses to diversify their vendor pool and helping alternative carriers gain market share from the large legacy carriers.
Fuel surcharges are a major cost driver this year for businesses that purchase parcel transportation. Diesel fuel prices have soared since the start of the Iran war in February, which slowed crude oil and refined fuel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, but repetitive carrier changes to the formula that sets fuel surcharges have more to do with elevated rates than the actual rise in fuel prices, the companies said in the benchmark report.
Carriers have frequently reindexed surcharge tables since 2021 to not only capture additional revenue as fuel prices rise, but keep fuel surcharges high even as actual fuel prices fall, according to the TD Cowen/AFS Freight Index released on Tuesday.
The fuel surcharge has increased from 7.75% of the transportation rate in the first quarter of 2021, when the average diesel fuel price was $2.91 per gallon, to 30% in September, when diesel peaked at $6.53 per gallon. Nearly three quarters of the increase is the result of carrier adjustments to fuel surcharge tables, not the price at the pump, the report said.
Even if fuel prices returned to the 2021 level, the current fuel surcharge would be 23.75% — about three times higher than five years ago.
The T D Cowen/AFS Freight Index has pointed all year to tinkering with the fuel-surcharge mechanism as a major cause of shipping inflation.
(Source: TD Cowen/AFS Freight Index)
“While diesel and jet fuel are major costs for ground and express parcel, the fuel surcharge has become a revenue lever for carriers in addition to a pass-through mechanism for covering the cost of doing business,” said Mingshu Bates, chief analytics officer and president of parcel at AFS Logistics, in a news release promoting the report. “Even if crude oil normalizes and fuel prices recede, the effective fuel surcharge will not show a material decrease.”
AFS Logistics uses transactional data to help companies manage their parcel, less-than-truckload and truckload freight costs.
New FedEx surcharges
Fuel isn’t the only area where large carriers make pricing changes that often go unnoticed by customers. Carriers have replaced predictable annual hikes with continuous, targeted pricing to protect margins even as overall demand growth slows, and are able to do so with limited pushback because most shippers still plan annually, industry practitioners say.
From the start of 2025 through mid-summer, FedEx implemented or announced more than 50 pricing changes , including general rate increases, delivery area surcharges, customs fees and demand surcharges, parcel spend management firm LJM previously reported.
For the fourth consecutive year, FedEx ( NYSE: FDX ) last month announced a 5.9% average general rate increase, effective Jan. 4. Embedded in the new pricing policy is a change that reclassifies 2,533 ZIP codes from extended delivery area surcharge to remote DAS — the most expensive tier. The change was much more extensive than an earlier one in which 102 ZIP codes were added to the standard delivery area surcharge tier, 74 moved from standard to extended area and 63 moved from extended to remote area.
For packages destined for ZIP codes reclassified from extended to remote, the DAS fee will jump to $17.75 — roughly doubling the fee for residential deliveries and more than tripling it for commercial destinations, the TD Cowen/AFS report said.
Shippers with high residential volume, rural deliveries, lightweight packages, or heavy accessorial exposure, the effective increase can expect materially higher shipping increases than 5.9%, warned Charles Moore, vice president of parcel solutions at Transportation Insight, on LinkedIn.
Ground pricing has flattened across zones, with increases almost uniform across all regions instead of just for long-haul routes. Lightweight e-commerce shipments take the biggest hit, with packages in the one-to-five pound range getting increases of nearly 6.5%, making small parcel shipping more expensive for many retailers. The FedEx Ground minimum charge is set to increase to $12.70, representing a compounded increase of more than 12% over the last two years. Additional handling fees are increasing between 7% and 7.6%, he pointed out. And FedEx is introducing a $25 Paper Document Fee and a $5 Paper Air Waybill Fee to reinforce the carrier’s push toward fully electronic shipping and trade documentation.
DHL eCommerce recently posted its peak season surcharges UPS ( NYSE: UPS ) has similarly hiked a broad spectrum of surcharges, including new cubic-volume rules, in recent years. Amazon, the U.S. Postal Service and more independent carriers are beginning to follow suit.
So far, DHL eCommerce, Amazon Shipping and OnTrac, besides FedEx, UPS and the USPS, have announced peak season surcharges. DHL eCommerce’s surcharge has three pricing windows, starting in late October. The highest charges are between Nov. 22 and Dec. 26, when package volume is at its most. Fees also change by distance.
Consultancy LJM recommends DHL customers model peak costs by shipping week, product, weight and zone. A single average per-package surcharge will no longer provide an accurate forecast, it said on its website.
“Introduced with unprecedented frequency and often with little warning, [accessorial] charges are now a preferred lever for increasing revenue-per-package. . . . A fundamental change is to blame. Carriers that for years pushed to gain market share now only want the shipments which are most profitable in their networks” and are implementing pricing strategies accordingly, wrote Josh Dunham, co-founder and CEO of shipping intelligence platform Reveel, in an online column . He recommended shippers expand their rotation of parcel carriers.
Q3 parcel rates
With peak shipping season and demand surcharges around the corner, the index for ground parcel rate per package in the fourth quarter is projected to reach a record of 43.3% above the January 2018 baseline — up 5.8% year over year and up 3.2% from the previous quarter, TD Cowen and AFS Logistics said.
Similarly, the express parcel index is estimated to set a record for the fifth consecutive quarter, reaching 20.3% this quarter, a 13.8% increase year over year.
Third-quarter express parcel cost per package increased 1.1% from the prior quarter on higher billed weight, more premium service mix and increased accessorial fees.
The average billed weight continued to increase, reflecting an ongoing decline in the share of lightweight shipments and carrier rating rule changes that raise billable weight.
The report’s authors said FedEx and UPS have more room to offer deeper customer discounts this year as their network streamlining and efficiency programs lower operating costs and boost margins. FedEx is moving further than UPS, with discounting skewed strongly toward large customers, while UPS increases were concentrated in the small and medium segments.
UPS has repeatedly stated that one of its strategic target markets is small-and-medium businesses , which often don’t have the wherewithal to manage all their logistics needs internally and can benefit from a carrier with value-added services.
Meanwhile, ground parcel cost per package declined 2% quarter over quarter as lower fuel surcharges, reduced accessorials and deeper discounting offset continued rate pressure, according to TD Cowen/AFS Logistics. The average effective fuel surcharge paid by shippers fell 4.7%, as diesel moderated through the first two months of the quarter before reaching a record-high in September.
With discounts, FedEx and UPS both favored large shippers over small and medium ones. With diesel prices reaching a historic-high late last month, the Freight Index predicted carriers are likely to make further fuel-related adjustments to capture the revenue windfall.

Photo: VesselFinder
By Gavin van Marle
14 October 2026
The US-Iran conflict and subsequent closure of the Hormuz Straits have upended the networks, and fleet deployment strategies, of the world’s three largest common feeder operators – and seen AD Ports’ Global Feeder Services significantly close the gap on the market leaders.
According to new analysis from Alphaliner, the Middle East conflict, now in its eighth month, has forced the two largest operators, X-Press Feeders and DP Worldm to reduce their offered capacity as the closure of Gulf routes curtailed their networks.
“X-Press Feeders remains the world’s largest feeder operator by deployed capacity, although its fleet has contracted by 7.1% year on year, as per Alphaliner’s survey on 21 September,” the analyst writes this week.
“Fallout from the Middle East conflict forced X-Press to make service cuts across the region, which is the main reason for the decline.”
Source: Alphaliner
As a result, X-Press Feeders’ global capacity is now 182,776 teu, down 13,987 teu from September 2025, with its capacity serving the Middle East region down 34.2% – equivalent to 38,000 teu – which Alphaliner linked to service suspension in the wake of the conflict.
To offset this, it has increased capacity in the intra-Europe trades by 7.4%, and intra-Americas by 17.7%, and has even taken the unusual step, for a feeder operator, of joining a deepsea Asia-Europe service, via the deployment of the 4,800 teu X-Press Odyssey on the China-Mediterranean CEX service, jointly run with China United Lines, Uniglory, and Global Feeder Services.
Meanwhile, DP World’s global capacity, largely made up of the Unifeeder fleet, fell 2.5% during the year, a “modest overall decline, also driven by the Middle East conflict”, said Alphaliner.
It added: “Its deployed capacity in the ME/ISC related trade fell by 7,500 teu, while its operated capacity in all other regions remained broadly stable year on year.
“Most of the cuts came from Gulf-related loops,” Alphaliner wrote, noting it had largely redeployed capacity to the Asia-India trade, as well as to a number of extra loaders serving the ME/ISC trade.
However, Emirati compatriot Global Feeder Services (GFS), owned by AD Ports, in what appears to be a commercial strategy that closely resembles that of DP World, saw its capacity jump by 31%, and its fleet is now only a fraction behind that of its rival – just 2,800 teu smaller – after it doubled-down on serving the India-Middle East trade corridor.
“The ME/ISC trade remains GFS’s core market and accounted for the bulk of its growth, in contrast to X-Press Feeders and DP World, which both reduced their presence there,” said Alphaliner, calculating that GFS’s capacity on that trade grew 26.9% and now accounts for around 70% of its total fleet.
“While its two main competitors scaled back in the region, GFS kept its network largely intact. The carrier replaced Gulf calls on existing loops with Red Sea ports, and extended its reach into neighbouring trades.
“As a result, GFS has overtaken both rivals to become the largest of the three in the ME/ISC trade, ahead of X-Press Feeders (about 73,500 teu) and DP World (about 70,500 teu),” the analyst added.

Want to be among the first to own Ford’s new EV pickup? You can now sign up for a preorder invite for the upcoming $30,000 Ford Fathom.
Ford Fathom preorder invites go live
Although preorders for the Fathom won’t officially open until early 2027, Ford is now inviting interested buyers to sign up for a preorder invite and become one of the first to own its all-new electric pickup.
The Fathom will start at $28,350 for the standard range battery model, or about half as much as the F-150 Lightning, Ford’s first attempt at an electric pickup. Even with the $1,595 destination fee, it will still start at under $30,000.
As the first model based on its new Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, Ford promises the Fathom will be a step change from its first-generation EVs.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Ford has yet to announce driving range figures, towing capability, and other key specs, but it did reveal a few details about the upcoming EV pickup.
Ford opens Fathom preorder invite list (Source: Ford.com)
For one, Ford previously said the Fathom will offer more passenger room than a Toyota RAV4, and that’s not including the frunk or truck bed. The company also claims it will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.
The interior will feature a “large touchscreen display” and will be the first to have Apple Maps directly integrated into the navigation system.
Other standard features include a Digital Key, Ford app remote control, and Apple CarPlay and Android Auto support.
Ford Fathom EV pickup prototype (Source: Jim Farley)
All Ford Fathom models will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free highway driving and will offer bidirectional charging capability.
It will use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to cut costs and vehicle weight, while also opening up interior space.
The cobalt-free and nickel-free LFP battery pack serves as the vehicle’s floor. As such, the low center of gravity improves handling and creates a quieter, more spacious interior.
Ford midsize EV pickup spotted testing in Arizona (Source: KindelAuto)
The low center of gravity, instant torque, and “obsessive chassis engineering” will make it fun to drive, Ford promises.
With even more downforce, Ford said the Fathom will have a targeted 0 to 60 mph time as fast as a Mustang EcoBoost.
Ford describes the Fathom as a “midsize, four-door electric pickup,” but the prototypes spotted testing appear to be about the size of a Maverick, which is generally considered a compact truck. Again, we’ll have to wait until closer to launch for final dimensions.
Covered Ford Fathom vehicle (Source: Ford)
We also know Ford’s upcoming EV pickup will have an NACS port after a few test mules were captured at a Tesla Supercharger over the summer.
You can sign up for your preorder invite on Ford’s website here to receive updates and to be among the first on the list.
Ford will officially open Fathom preorders in early 2027. The first Fathom prototypes are scheduled to roll off the production line at its 3-million-square-foot Louisville Assembly Plant (LAP) in 2027, with deliveries expected to begin later in the year.
CEO Jim Farley admitted at the 2026 Automotive News Congress a few weeks ago that “It’s going to be a heck of an effort to launch this at scale, at cost, on time.”
A Ford spokesperson confirmed with Electrek , however, that “We’ve said previously, ‘Fathom will launch in 2027’ – and there is no change to that.”
We should learn more about Ford’s upcoming EV pickup soon. Stay tuned for the latest updates.

Image: Sunrun
Tesla Powerwalls did most of the heavy lifting as California’s home batteries set a new grid record last week. On October 6, more than 85,000 Powerwall owners sent over 600 MW to the grid, the bulk of a combined 745 MW dispatch that Sunrun announced today.
That’s 28% more than the 580 MW record the two companies set less than a month ago. And it’s bigger than most gas peaker plants in the state.
Tesla posted its record first
Tesla Energy put out its own numbers on October 8, two days after the event. The company said 85,000+ Powerwall owners across California dispatched more than 600 MW to help meet peak demand, calling it “a new record for the largest Powerwall VPP event.”
Sunrun followed this morning with a release that has Sunrun “leading” the dispatch. It says “the companies” delivered 669 MW on October 5 and 745 MW on October 6, but it doesn’t break out how much came from Sunrun customers versus Tesla customers.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Put Tesla’s figure against Sunrun’s total and Powerwalls account for roughly 80% of the record. In September, the share was even higher: 517 MW of the 580 MW came from about 110,000 Powerwalls , and Sunrun owns or operates 55% of those.
So both companies are taking a victory lap for largely the same batteries. Sunrun is the biggest Powerwall channel in the country, which is why the two keep showing up in each other’s press releases.
There’s also an interesting detail in Tesla’s math. Just over 600 MW from about 85,000 homes works out to roughly 7 kW per home, well above the 5 kW continuous output of a Powerwall 2. That points to a fleet increasingly made of Powerwall 3 units, rated at 11.5 kW, and homes with more than one battery.
How the dispatch worked
The events came during an October heat wave, at the request of the California Energy Commission and the state’s utilities. Batteries discharged through multi-hour evening peaks to cut demand and push down real-time power prices.
Sunrun says October 5 was the first event this year where the state’s Demand Side Grid Support (DSGS) and Emergency Load Reduction Program (ELRP) both called dispatches at the same time across every participating investor-owned utility territory. DSGS kicks in once CAISO’s day-ahead price passes $200/MWh.
According to Sunrun, 745 MW is enough to cover every household in San Francisco and San Jose combined during peak hours. The company now has more than 120,000 home batteries enrolled in California grid programs.
The pace is what stands out. The previous residential record, 539 MW, stood from July 29, 2025, until September 9, 2026. It grew 8% in over a year, then 28% in four weeks.
Customers get paid for this, too. Sunrun CEO Mary Powell said “customers are being compensated for helping strengthen grid reliability.”
Next up: San Jose
Sunrun also says a Google-funded distributed power plant with PG&E in the San Jose area plans to enroll nearly 21,000 devices with Tesla and Everyday Electric, the company formerly known as Renew Home. Initial dispatches are expected this month.
It’s the first concrete piece of the 16.8 GW virtual power plant plan for data centers that Tesla, Sunrun, and Renew Home announced in June. But it’s early: Sunrun notes the Tesla and Everyday Electric part of the project is still under a non-binding letter of intent.
Electrek’s Take
Tesla’s real advantage shows up here: a huge installed base and software that gets 85,000+ homes to respond to the same grid signal at once. Nobody else in residential storage is close.
The credit grab between Tesla and Sunrun is a bit silly. It’s one fleet, mostly Powerwalls, with Sunrun as the biggest owner. Fine. Both deserve it.
What I’d really like to see is energy, not just power. Both companies report MW, and neither gives MWh or exact duration. A 745 MW peak for 20 minutes and 745 MW held for three hours are very different things for the grid. The September event ran a three-hour evening window, which is good. Publishing MWh every time would make the case even stronger.
And this works because California pays for it. DSGS and ELRP put real money in homeowners’ pockets for discharging at the right time. Most states have nothing like it, so these batteries just sit there during peaks.
If you’ve got a Powerwall or are thinking of getting one, pairing it with solar is how you get the most value out of it, and in California it can now get you paid by the grid. He Bought a New Chevy Corvette in April 2026 and He Wants It Gone After Less Than 700 Miles
14 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
There are countless Chevrolet Corvette blue-collar supercars looking for new homes on the used car market at any given moment in most parts of the world, and even more in the States, and this C8 Stingray is just one of them.
So, what caught our attention that made us dedicate an entire story to it? The fact that it is brand new, yet its owner wants it gone. What is the reason, you ask? Well, that’s a very good question, though we do not know the answer. If you do, feel free to drop a line below. What we can tell you is that the man bought it in April 2026, adding less than 700 miles (1,125 km) since.
In fact, the digital odometer revealed 686 miles (1,104 km) at the time of cataloging, and that translates to a little over 100 miles (160 km) per month on average since the car left the dealership. The seller paid $83,965 for this 2026 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray , which is a Coupe 2LT in case you were wondering, and now he wants it gone, hence why he listed it for sale as part of an ongoing auction on Cars&Bids.
Before moving on to the details, we will tell you that a used C8 Chevy Corvette normally sells for $50,000 to $90,000 in today’s used car market. We have seen some examples that broke into the $40,000 zone, and those were earlier model years. Later model years tend to fetch over $80,000, and it is not uncommon to see some change hands for more than $90,000. Thus, it all comes down to the model year, mileage, and specification, and you should keep in mind that convertibles are a bit more expensive than coupes.
Photo: Cars&Bids On average, the 2026 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray Coupe 2LT fetches between $75,000 and $86,000, and it will be interesting to see how much this example gets when the gavel hits the table six days from now, on October 20, 2026. Since we have told you about the Benjamins, we should also tell you that the highest bid at the time of writing was $10,100, and there is obviously a reserve on it that clearly hasn’t been met.
Finished in Blade Silver Metallic, this Chevrolet Corvette Stingray has a Sky Cool Gray interior. It features 19-inch wheels at the front and 20-inch wheels at the rear, has a removable roof panel, heated and ventilated seats, yellow seatbelts, leather upholstery, a head-up display, a Bose sound system, and a performance data and video recorder for extra fun at the local racetrack, the listing reveals.
This ‘Vette does not feature the newer motor, which is a small-black 6.7-liter V8. The LS6 is officially good for 535 hp (453 ps/399 kW ) and 520 lb-ft (705 Nm) of torque in the 2027 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray . With the optional Z51 Performance Pack, the car hits 60 mph (97 kph) in just 2.8 seconds, though some tests have revealed that it is a bit faster than that. It completes the standing quarter mile in 11 seconds at 124 mph (200 kph), and taps out at over 200 mph (322+ kph).
Photo: Cars&Bids Powering the pictured Corvette is the old 6.2-liter V8, which is rated at 490 horsepower (497 ps/365 kW). Thus, the car does not feature the Performance Exhaust System or the Z51 Performance Package, as if it did, then it would have had 495 hp (502 ps/369 kW). The output is channeled to the rear wheels through an eight-speed automatic transmission. This model hit 60 mph (97 kph) in as little as 2.9 seconds, and ran the quarter mile in over 11 seconds from a standstill.
Due to the extremely low mileage, this Chevrolet Corvette Stingray has not required servicing, and there is nothing wrong with it, as the car is in top-notch condition. Besides the vehicle, is offered with a clean Carfax history report, and has a clean Florida title, the next owner will also get two keys, the window sticker, and the owner’s manual. The seller noted that the tires carry 2026 and 2025 date code tires, and that’s nothing to be worried about, obviously, as the only thing this ride needs is gasoline in the tank a petrolhead behind the wheel.
We are curious to find out how much this rear mid-engined, rear-wheel drive blue-collar supercar will fetch once the gavel hits the table on the ongoing online auction, so we will keep an eye on the listing. And if you want to spruce up your life with the pictured Corvette, then you should check it out in more detail here on the quoted website. That is also where you can bid on it.
But realistically speaking, how much would you pay for this machine, knowing that you could get a brand-new ‘Vette with the new motor from $71,300 (MSRP)?

A Heavy Expanded Mobility Tactical Truck and one of the launchers assigned to 1st Battalion, 51st Air Defense Artillery, 1st Multi-Domain Task Force, participates in new equipment fielding, training, and gunnery certification of the Integrated Fires Protection Capability (IFPC) on Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Wash., Nov. 20, 2025. (U.S. Army photo by Staff Sgt. Brandon Rickert)
WASHINGTON — After tapping two teams to continue development for a second interceptor for its Indirect Fire Protection Capability (IFPC) Increment 2 launcher, the Army is creating a way for other vendors to keep competing, according to a three-star general.
Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano the Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires described the effort as an “off-shoot opportunity” that the service will pursue even as it works with competition winners Lockheed Martin and a team-up from Boeing and Anduril. The opportunity would allow for another competition planned for the fourth quarter of 2027.
“We wanted to turn up the heat on that program,” Lozano told an audience Tuesday at the annual Association of the US Army conference. “I want to run an in parallel, what I call an in-strike competition.”
“We basically just said, ‘Hey, if there’s any other company who didn’t make the first cut … but oh by the way, [if] you continue to invest in its second interceptor capability, we’d love for you to come out to the range,’” he later added. “We’ll give you range time. We’ll present targets and will allow you to recompete with an opportunity to get back into the program fold.”
The service is using the same set up for the for next generation short-range interceptor program, allowing other companies to compete against Lockheed and Raytheon who are under contracts with the Army and competing for a production deal.
The move comes as the Pentagon looks for ways to ramp up critical munition production and refill its stockpiles. In recent months the department has inked a series of framework agreements designed to pave the path of multi-year contracts.
A Question Of Budgets
When it comes to Army programs, acquisition czar Brent Ingraham told the same audience that the service will need to see where the 2027 defense budget lands and make sure these munition deals are a funding priority.
The challenge for the Army and other services is, in part, centered on the administration’s decision to place a large swath of the munition buy inside a reconciliation request instead of the base budget. Lawmakers are not yet moving forward with that reconciliation request and defense officials may reshuffle the base budget request.
“Depending on where a budget lands, what a top line looks like, whether there’s a reconciliation or not … all those things will drive us to figure out how we ensure that we continue to give the right demand signal to industry” on critical munitions, Ingraham said.
Despite the rash of framework agreements, he acknowledged, “I can’t expect industry to sort of invest like we’ve been asking them to invest on a wish list or a dream.”
Should the CR run for a full year, the Army may need to “reprioritize” funds to make sure the dollars are there to support the multi-year buys, he said.

Obesity-focused Zealand Pharma is buying into Generate:Biomedicines’s generative AI platform to create new multispecific drug candidates.
Zealand Pharma is enlisting Generate:Biomedicines and its AI-driven drug design platform to develop treatments for weight loss and metabolic conditions in a deal that could reach up to $1.2 billion.
The agreement, announced Tuesday , includes a $30 million upfront payment from Zealand, plus up to $35 million in early preclinical milestones. Generate could collect almost $1.2 billion in total development, regulatory and commercial milestones, plus tiered royalties on sales of any alliance asset that reaches the market.
For its investment, Danish biopharma Zealand gains access to Generate’s generative AI platform to design new protein therapeutics for obesity and other metabolic diseases. Generate will be responsible for all research activities through candidate selection, while Zealand will take charge of clinical development, as well as regulatory and commercialization activities.
With one of the most mature pipelines among its peers, Generate is at the leading edge of a growing class of drugmakers using generative AI to design drugs. Founded in 2018 by Flagship Pioneering, the biotech’s approach “infers generalizable principles of biology” to design potentially therapeutic molecules targeting some of the most difficult-to-crack conditions, according to the company’s website .
Massachusetts-based Generate went public in February with $425 million—money meant to support the Phase 3 development of its anti-TSLP therapy GB-0895 for severe asthma. GB-0895, which is also in early-stage studies for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), was designed using the company’s generative AI platform.
Phase 1 data disclosed last month showed that a single subcutaneous injection of GB-0895 led to “rapid and sustained reductions” in asthma biomarkers through six months of follow-up. The anti-TSLP antibody likewise lowered disease biomarkers in COPD. Tolerability, the study’s primary outcome , was also favorable, with treatment-emergent adverse events balanced between GB-0895 and placebo groups.
Generate’s pipeline also includes two cancer candidates: the MMAE-targeting antibody GB-4362 and the armored CAR T therapy GB-5267. Both are in early-stage development. Generate also has platform collaborations with Novartis and Amgen, through which the AI drugmaker will design novel therapies for a host of confidential programs.

For Zealand, the Generate agreement comes after an underwhelming readout last week for the long-acting amylin analog petrelintide. In the Phase 2 ZUPREME-2 study, which assessed weight loss at 28 weeks, patients on petrelintide saw up to a 9.2% mean weight loss versus 2% for placebo comparators. A total of 220 patients with obesity or overweight who also had type 2 diabetes were enrolled in the study.
While ZUPREME-2 hit its main goal, analysts at William Blair said they were “disappointed” that petrelintide did not elicit greater weight loss.
Also leaving analysts wanting was the reduction in A1c, a measure of average blood sugar levels—the drug reduced A1c by up to 0.65% versus a 0.23% increase in placebo. William Blair at the time pointed to A1c reductions seen with rival therapies such as Eli Lilly’s Zepbound and Novo’s Wegovy ranging from 1.3% to 2.1%.
Petrelintide is being developed in collaboration with Roche, which in March 2025 paid $1.65 billion upfront to license the asset and study it with the pharma’s own obesity candidate CT-388. The partners in September launched the Phase 3 ZUPREME program for petrelintide, aiming to enroll around 7,000 patients total.
Earlier this month, Zealand reported another obesity disappointment, this time for the Boehringer Ingelheim–partnered survodutide. The companies touted up to 13.1% weight loss at 76 weeks in patients taking the glucagon/GLP-1 receptor dual agonist—findings that investors found underwhelming, sending Zealand’s shares down 8% in the aftermath. 1993 Chevy C1500 Looks Almost Stock, but There's Something Special Under the Hood
24 photos
Photo: Autotopia LA | YouTube
This 1993 Chevrolet C1500 454 SS could have ended up in the crusher or be rotting in a backyard somewhere. However, life took a turn for the better for the good, old Chevy. Now, it rocks the streets, looking like the perfect sleeper, but roaring out all the drama of the big-block V8, which throws over 700 horsepower to the ground.
The man who is to blame for the build is Diego of Diego Creations. He bought a1993 Chevy C1500 454 SS Old Body Style (OBS), which was almost entirely stock at the time, and converted it into a street monster. The truck had the original big-block engine under the hood, but it had been bored out to 496. That changed along the way, but the exterior remained the same, as Diego wanted to keep the patina.
When General Motors initially launched the C1500 454 SS in 1990, it was offered exclusively in Onyx Black over a Garnet Red interior. In 1992 and 1993, GM expanded the lineup to include Summit White and Victory Red.
Because 1993 was the final and lowest-production year for the 454 SS, finding a factory-original Summit White truck with the original red interior makes it exceptionally rare, with production estimates tracking right around 65 units ever built in that specific combination.
Photo: Autotopia LA | YouTube This 1993 Chevrolet C1500 454 SS is one of the 65 built that year with a rare color combination: Summit White over a red interior. It was the rarity that convinced Diego to keep the interior and exterior as stock as possible. To lock in the surviving factory paint, Diego covered it with a Poppy's Patina clear coat.
Underneath, though, it is a whole different truck. It all starts with the LS3 416-cubic-inch V8 stroker engine, which has been fully built, still featuring the stock heads, but ported and polished, and sporting a modified crankshaft, forged H-beam connecting rods, and forged high-compression pistons.
The stock LSA blower with a Harrop lid kept its ground. The setup makes 715 horsepower to the wheels, which means around 900 horsepower at the crank. That is light-years away from the factory rating of the Chevy C1500 454 SS from back in the 1990s.
The truck rolled off the production line of the General Motors Fort Wayne Assembly Plant in Fort Wayne, Indiana, with the 454-cubic-inch (7.4-liter) big-block V8, which produced 255 horsepower (259 metric horsepower) and 405 pound-feet (549 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Autotopia LA | YouTube Those were enough to make it accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in just 7.2 seconds. It may not sound like much now that pickup trucks come with supercar figures, but back in the day, it was remarkably quick, especially because the V8 had to push forward a vehicle that tipped the scales at 4,500 pounds (2,041 kilograms).
Top speed was electronically limited from the factory to 110 mph (161 kph). It was not only the electronic governor programmed by GM into the computer chip to cut fuel around that speed, but also the brick-like aerodynamics that limited it.
A custom-made can from New Era sits under the hood, hosting the expansion tank, the cooling tank, and the catch can. The stock 4L80E four-speed automatic transmission with a torque converter puts the power down through the rear wheels. The stock driveshaft and stock rear end, shortened with Dutchman axles, are part of the plan.
Diego and his friends rebuilt the suspension, installed new front and rear coilovers as part of a QA1 Stage 3 coilover conversion kit, firewall tubs, and drivetrain. Diego came up with jumper ports in the load bed for those 'just in case' moments. A Twisted MetalWorkz fuel tank replaced the original one.
Photo: Autotopia LA | YouTube The truck rides on Bogart wheels, measuring 20 x 9 inches with 265/40 20" tires up front and 21 x 11.5 inches with 315/30 20" rubber out back, while 16-inch Wilwood disc brakes with six-piston calipers at all four corners provide the stopping power.
The red fabric-wrapped seats on board the truck remind Shawn of Autotopia LA of grandma's couch. Diego wouldn’t change that for the world. Dakota Digital gauges indicate all the relevant driving data. They mimic the factory 1993 analog layout when the truck is off, but light up with modern digital readouts when fired up. The truck is missing the center console, but Diego will come up with one. The original one succumbed to age.
On the road, with Shawn in the driver’s seat and Diego, for the first time, in the passenger seat, the LS3-powered truck is the perfect cruiser, quiet and comfortable. When you step on it, it loses good manners, but remains super responsive and predictable. On launch, it spins the tires like no tomorrow, leaving a cloud of smoke as it drives off. Not many ICEs out there can keep up with it.

Kawasaki KLX300 Gets Engine Surgery for 2027, New XPL Model Joins the Range
17 photos
Photo: Kawasaki
It’s a pretty busy week for Japanese bike maker Kawasaki, which announced on Wednesday a long list of returning motorcycles for the 2027 model year, with little to no changes to speak of. Alongside them came news of significant changes for other model families, including this here KLX300 dual-purpose machine.
To get the range ready for more adventures, the Japanese bike maker first and foremost made changes to the engine that powers the KLX300. Technically the same 292cc liquid-cooled, single-cylinder unit as before, it has been revised to improve responsiveness, performance, and power.
In a nutshell, Kawasaki performed engine surgery to install a plain bearing connecting rod, went for cam profiles sourced from the KLX300R off-road motorcycle, and installed an electrofusion cylinder with an ultra-hard coating. It’s unclear, in numbers, how these upgrades alter the engine behavior.
The engine is held inside a steel perimeter frame with an aluminum swingarm, with the entire bike supported by a 43 mm inverted cartridge-style fork at the front (ten inches of travel) and a new Uni-Trak suspension setup at the rear, delivering 9.1 inches of travel.
Kawasaki has also added ABS across the range, with the one deployed on dual-purpose models allowing itself to be disabled when traveling off the beaten path. There’s new digital instrumentation at the front of the bike, and the possibility of connecting a smartphone via Kawasaki’s dedicated app
The above modifications involve the entire KLX300 range, including the new XPL ABS that hits the market in tandem with the revised range. This variant has been specifically designed to be used on longer rides, and, as such, it comes packed full of features meant to facilitate that.
The bike is fitted, for instance, with a tall windshield to better protect the rider, hand guards, and a standard rear carrier with built-in tie-down hooks. There is a round LED headlight that makes it look all special, alongside the dedicated graphics centered on a brush pattern that mirrors the one on the KX motocross rides of the 1980s and 1990s.
In all, there are four different KLX300 bikes that can be had in the 2027 model year, all of which will become available by the first month of next year. Among them is a second new variant, the Durable Force (DF) ABS, which adds, on top of what the standard KLX300 ABS has to offer, new colors for the bodywork and special graphics.
